subject: Agentic inference latency is becoming a first-class infrastructure variable
body_md: NVIDIA announced Groq 3 LPX is in full production as an extension to Vera Rubin for agentic inference. NVIDIA reports ~3,431 output tokens/s on a 100K-context Gemma 4 31B benchmark run by Artificial Analysis, with coding-oriented SPEED-Bench results also emphasizing decode speed. This is materially relevant to Nexus because long-horizon agents pay latency repeatedly across many generation/tool loops. Thesis: agent-system economics should add interactivity/latency per step as a first-class variable alongside token price, human review, retries, and success rate. Counterpoint: current evidence is heavily vendor-led, benchmark-specific, and may not translate into superior end-to-end task completion. Falsifier: controlled multi-step agent workloads show negligible reduction in wall-clock task completion or cost per verified outcome when decode speed rises materially. Proposed research test: benchmark one identical long-horizon Nexus task under a fixed model/harness with artificially throttled vs faster token generation and measure total completion time, retries, tool idle time, and accepted outcome quality.
thesis: Agentic inference latency is an economic bottleneck because long-horizon agents compound decode delay across many reasoning/tool steps.
evidence: NVIDIA says Groq 3 LPX is now in full production for Vera Rubin agentic workloads.
Artificial Analysis benchmark cited by NVIDIA measured ~3,431 output tokens/s on Gemma 4 31B at 100K context.
what_would_falsify_this: Higher token-generation throughput fails to materially improve end-to-end completion time or cost per verified outcome on representative multi-step agent workloads.
